letters.incipit: My most dearly esteemed mother,
Most Honourable, In the first beginning of this duty
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to Lord Zouche from Ingolstadt on October 27, 1590, providing an update on his diplomatic observations. He describes his reception upon delivering Lord Zouche’s letters, noting his interactions with Hubert van Giffen, a prominent jurist at Ingolstadt. Wotton then recounts his encounter with a disgraced Englishman—likely Anthony Sherley—who resents Queen Elizabeth I, blaming her for confiscating his family’s estates and spreading anti-Elizabethan rhetoric. Wotton implies that this Englishman has received “dangerous advice” from his father and suggests that his presence abroad is politically motivated rather than merely personal. The letter also contains intelligence about the papal election, reporting the false news that Cardinal di Santa Severina had been elected Pope under the name Julius IV. He notes the Jesuit College’s reaction to the election, implying Jesuit influence in the process. Wotton promises to send more details from Vienna and closes by reaffirming his loyalty to Lord Zouche.

letters.abstract: Wotton reports his arrival at Vienna, his circumstances there, the Austrian Archdukes, and European political news.

letters.marked: 17th of April, CIↃIↃXCI. Style of Rome.
letters.incipit: My most Honoured dear Lord, I received your last from Altorph the 24th of March,
My most Honoured Lord, I have this present returned unto your Honour
letters.abstract: In this letter, dated April 21, 1591, from Vienna, Henry Wotton updates Lord Zouche on various matters, including his return of a book of arms and descents and his difficulties obtaining an architectural model. He describes his failed attempt to secure a drawing of a Lusthaus (pleasure house) from a master architect, who had lent the model to an Italian. Wotton suspects that the architect still possesses it but requires a bribe. Additionally, he reports a discovered plot in Graz to massacre Lutherans, possibly orchestrated by Rome, and how it was foiled when a messenger mistakenly delivered incriminating documents to the wrong Chapel Master. He also provides a colorful account of an Englishman in Vienna, Abraham Miller, whose misadventures reflect both personal folly and the broader tensions between the English and the Austrians regarding employment opportunities.

letters.incipit: Any point in this that concerns myself, I beseech that no man may see but your Honour. My most Honoured Lord,
Most Honoured Lord, Since my last, written unto your Honour from Florence
letters.abstract: This letter from Wotton to Lord Zouche reports on Wotton’s personal illness, the visit of Archduke Maximilian to Rome, and the broader political maneuvering surrounding his visit. Wotton describes Maximilian’s humble attire upon his arrival in Rome, emphasizing his religious piety and the clandestine nature of his interactions with Jesuits and Cardinal Madrutz. The Pope, having recently staged an illness due to a prior political incident, was hesitant to meet the Archduke but eventually did so. There is speculation about the purpose of Maximilian’s visit. Some believed it was to prevent the marriage between the King of Poland (Sigismund III) and a daughter of Austria, but others dismissed this theory in favor of the idea that Maximilian sought Papal intervention to pressure the Emperor into abdicating either the Roman or Hungarian crown in his favor. The letter also notes that the Pope presented Maximilian with a religious relic and a gold medaglia, laden with indulgences—a gesture Wotton dismisses with sarcasm. On a personal note, Wotton discusses his continued residence in Florence at the house of Bacchio Boni, his financial concerns, and his likely stay in Italy over the summer. The letter closes with a request to remain informed of any relevant political affairs.

letters.incipit: Most Honourable, I received your letters of the third of June,
Most Honourable, . . . Out of England I have received no letters since my last unto your Honour,
Most Honourable, My last I sent by a Dutch gentleman,
Most Honourable, Your letters of the first of July I received the sixteenth of the same.
letters.abstract: This letter, written on July 27th 1592, presents a report by Henry Wotton to Baron Edward La Zouche, detailing the recent affairs in Rome and France from the last week. The author presents the rumours surrounding the possible cardinalship of Archbishop of Pisa, as well as activities of Pope Clement VIII (particularly his general examination of the clergy in the church of St. John Lateran). The letter also touches upon the topic of the French Wars of Religion, mentioning the actions of the Duke of Parma and Duke of Mayn (Mayenne).
mentions: Dutch gentleman|Cesare d'Este, Duke of Modena

letters.incipit: Most Honourable, Your last, written on the 29th of July, came to me on the 6th of August;
letters.abstract: This letter, written on August 14th 1592, presents a report by Henry Wotton to Baron Edward La Zouche, detailing the recent affairs in Europe, particularly Florence, where the author is stationed, and England, from where came news of a regicide plot by Mary Queen of Scots. Codenames are given for certain figures to be used in later correspondence. The author also touches upon more personal matters, mainly concerning the activities of his brothers, one of whom has recently lost his wife.
mentions: Anne of Denmark, Queen of Scotland

letters.incipit: My ever most Honoured, . . . Since my last unto your Honour (contrary to the expectation of all)
letters.abstract: This letter, written on August 29th 1592, presents a report by Henry Wotton to Baron Edward La Zouche, detailing the recent affairs in Europe, starting with the political marriage of Leonora Ursina and rumours surrounding it. The author speaks also of the situation in Rome, where Pope has executed a few people for sodomy and a gruesome murder was committed. Two new bans (bandi) are discussed, one against Jews and another against Spanish courtesans. The letter also relates the movements of several European officials, Baron of Bernstein and John de Taxis.

letters.incipit: My most Honoured Lord, We have this week little store of either rumour or effect.
letters.abstract: This letter, written on September 6th 1592, presents a report by Henry Wotton to Baron Edward La Zouche, detailing the recent affairs in Italy, The letter narrates the aftermath of a recent battle near Mantua, mentions a plague in Vienna, and briefly touches upon the topic of the correspondence of John de Taxis, aka Thomas Darcy, 3rd Lord of Chiche. The author speaks about the state of his mission in Italy, currently awaiting further orders and planning to depart to France after six months and stay there for a year.
mentions: Christine de Lorraine, Grand Duchess of Tuscany
Court of the Grand Duke of Tuscany

letters.incipit: My most Honoured Lord, . . . I am preparing to remove to Sienna,
letters.abstract: This letter, written on September 19th 1592, presents a report by Henry Wotton to Baron Edward La Zouche, detailing the recent affairs in Italy. The author presents his plans to leave Florence in the upcoming days and travel to Sienna. He also informs of the arrival Lord Darcy (codename: John de Taxis) to Florence.

letters.incipit: Most Honourable, Your last of the second of September I received the twenty-third of the same.

letters.marked: twenty-fifth of October, 1592, style of Rome
letters.incipit: Most Honourable, Through Prato, Pistoia, Luca, Pisa, and most of the towns which are situate in the plain of Hetruria,
Most Honourable, I have, for fourteen days,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to Lord Zouche regarding political and religious intrigue surrounding Lord Darcy in Rome. Darcy, accused of possessing a controversial book by Jesuit Antonio Possevino, faced scrutiny from the Inquisition. The Grand Duke of Tuscany intervened on his behalf, but fears arose that the book’s reprinting would provoke further reprisals. Additionally, Wotton notes accusations of secret correspondences between French exiles and Cardinal Mendoza, potentially leading to severe consequences. Wotton also updates Zouche on his personal situation, including financial concerns, delays in his journey to Venice, and false rumors of his imprisonment by the Inquisition.

letters.incipit: Most Honourable Lord, In my last unto your Honour from this town,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes from Sienna to Lord Zouche, discussing encrypted correspondence and intercepted letters. He informs Zouche of two books published in Italy against the Lord Treasurer, allegedly connected to a Catholic network involving English contacts. He also describes his recent interactions with Cardinal Robert Bellarmine and his hesitancy about revealing their conversation. Additionally, he comments on European political affairs, including a potential marriage alliance between the Medici and Bavaria, and notes the presence of Jesuits at the courts of Bavarian princes.

letters.incipit: Most Honourable, Having in my three last unto your Honour signified by cipher certain dangerous points,
letters.abstract: Wotton reports on political and ecclesiastical matters, particularly the unexpected decision by the Pope not to create new cardinals, despite anticipation. He notes that this primarily affects Father Toledo, who was expected to benefit. He discusses the recent deaths of several cardinals, including Canano and Mondovio, as well as the implications for papal politics. The letter also touches on the travels of two Bavarian princes and their reception at Caprarola, possibly as part of papal maneuvering. There is mention of ongoing shifts within the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, including Don Pietro de’ Medici’s marriage in Spain and Signieur Silvio’s new naval appointment.

letters.marked: 23 of May, 1603. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right honourable, The good opinion which it has pleased your Honour first to conceive in your self of me,
Sir, The enclosed unto you from my Lord Cecyll is rather of course a necessity,
Right Honourable and my very good Lord, This State resolved to send for me
I shall be called to-morrow (as I hear, though I am not yet warned)
Your Lordship receiveth herein (apart from other businesses)
letters.abstract: This letter, written by Henry Wotton to Viscount Cranborne in May 1605 from Venice, discusses intelligence matters related to the political situation in Italy and Spain. Wotton informs Cranborne about the uncertain status of the papal election following the death of Clement VIII, the return of the Jesuit Robert Parsons to Rome, and the broader Spanish influence in the region. He describes his deployment of two agents—Rowland Woodward, sent to Milan, and George Rooke, sent to Naples—both involved in espionage regarding Spanish military and political maneuvers. Wotton expresses concern about Parsons’ activities and their implications for English interests.
mentions: Court of James VI and I
Pedro Henriquez de Acevedo, Count of Fuentes

letters.incipit: Here is nothing yet determined in the late deliberations
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton informs Robert Cecil, Viscount Cranborne, of the ongoing deliberations in Venice regarding maritime piracy and the English response to Venetian naval interference. He discusses the case of Nicolo Balbi, a Venetian accused of murdering an English merchant, Nicholas Pardoe, and emphasizes his role as both an accuser and a negotiator in securing justice for the victim. Wotton details his exchanges with Advocate Finetti, Balbi’s legal defender, noting his attempts to persuade Balbi to confess and deliver the stolen money and documents. He stresses his diplomatic balancing act—ensuring that Venice does not perceive English intervention as an overreach while still maintaining England’s demand for justice. Wotton expresses confidence that Balbi will not escape punishment unless unforeseen circumstances intervene. He also briefly mentions that the papal conclave remains unresolved and that Robert Parsons, the prominent English Jesuit, has returned to Rome, hinting at further intelligence to be conveyed to the English crown.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: I have likewise received the second from your Lordship of the 15 of June
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to Sir Thomas Edmondes, the English ambassador in Brussels, with updates from Venice. He comments on the uncertain state of the papacy, describing the new Pope as financially driven, favoring Spain over France due to monetary considerations. Wotton also reports on the murder of Mr. Arthur Poole in Rome, a mysterious and violent death involving three wounds but leaving valuable possessions untouched, raising suspicions about the nature of the crime. Poole was given an elaborate burial at the Jesuit College under the direction of Cardinal Farnese. The letter closes with Wotton excusing himself from writing in his own hand due to the oppressive heat, dictating the letter instead.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and My Very Good Lord, The report being come hither from divers places,
letters.abstract: In this letter, dated August 18, 1605, Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury about reports of Catholic agitation in Wales and broader concerns regarding the influence of Rome on English subjects. He warns that the Catholic party is growing and expresses anxiety over the conversion efforts of Jesuits, seminary priests, and other Catholic missionaries. Wotton frames this religious activity as a form of corruption, suggesting that the Pope and Jesuits are engaged in a systematic effort to undermine England’s Protestant stability. He contrasts past papal approaches, particularly those of Sixtus V and Clement VIII, arguing that the latter encouraged religious infiltration rather than violent persecution. The letter reflects a conspiratorial tone, portraying Catholic influence as a covert and organized threat. Wotton also comments on the diplomatic maneuvers of Pope Paul V, particularly his relationship with King James I, and mentions figures such as Monsignor Paulino, who appears to be maneuvering within the papal court. The letter exemplifies how early modern diplomatic correspondence blended intelligence gathering with political and religious anxieties, demonstrating both real geopolitical concerns and conspiratorial thinking.

letters.incipit: My very good Lord, I have indeed (as your Lordship did courteously conjecture in your last of the 21 of September) been in villa,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to Sir Thomas Edmondes, the English ambassador in Brussels, with brief updates from Venice, where he returned to after September villeggiatura. He relates the current state of the city, now full with representatives of European monarchies and noble families, particularly those from France and Spain.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I have stayed the dispatching of that gentleman
letters.abstract: In this letter Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury about the sickness of the Prince Grimani, Doge of Venice.

letters.incipit: My very good Lord, I have had no letters from your Lordship these three weeks.
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to Sir Thomas Edmondes, the English ambassador in Brussels, with news about the death of Prince Grimani, Doge of Venice, as well as the information concerning his succession.

letters.marked: last of December, 1605. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Sir, I have, since your departure from hence
My very good Lord, I have received from your Lordship no letters these last two months

letters.marked: 17 of February, 1605⟨6⟩. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: In this business there are two remedies,
Right Honourable and my very good Lord, Marino Grimani, Duke of Venice
Sir, I have received your last of the seventh of February,
letters.abstract: In this letter of 24 February 1606, Henry Wotton writes to Edward Barrett discussing news related to Sir Robert Dudley and Elizabeth Southwell. He remarks on the role of Captain Eliot in facilitating their unlawful marriage, suggesting that papal authorities may accuse him of procedural misconduct, motivated not by moral considerations, but by the scandalous nature of the situation. Wotton expresses sympathy for Southwell, portraying her as noble but misled, and asks Barrett to convey his respects should he meet her, to which Wotton encourages him. Turning to Venetian affairs, Wotton describes the uncertain political climate, marked by reluctance toward war but deep divisions preventing resolution. He recounts in detail the recent arrival and reception of Cardinal Joyeuse as French ambassador extraordinary, noting the carefully staged ceremonial honors accorded to him both as ambassador and cardinal. He highlights the unusually discreet handling of the Cardinal’s private audience, contrasting it with typical French display as well as ostentiation shown previously by the Spanish side, interpreting it as a strategic gesture. Wotton anticipates that Joyeuse’s proposals will soon be presented to the Senate but expresses skepticism that any statements made on behalf of the Pope will carry weight, given his formal role as a representative of the French crown. He concludes with friendly greetings and a request for further updates regarding Dudley and Southwell.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: Sir, I have received your judgement upon the Spanish accident,
letters.abstract: In this letter dated 3 March 1606/7, Henry Wotton thanks Edward Barrett for his analysis of a recent Spanish incident and reports news from across Europe. He relays that the Spanish king is expected to execute the Count of Villa Lunga. He notes a lack of significant updates from England, but describes military preparations in France, where the king is mobilizing forces in order to march to Lyon, as well as developments in the Low Countries, including the supposed capture of Count Frederick van den Berg by Henry of Nassau. Turning to Venice, Wotton anticipates the imminent arrival of the Duke of Savoy and the Marquis of Castiglione as imperial envoys, adding to the already complex diplomatic environment involving French, Spanish, and Imperial representatives. He remarks on his own solitary position as England’s representative amid these competing powers. Wotton suggests that Barrett consider traveling to Italy to witness these significant events firsthand and asks him to first send him some Tuscan olives. He concludes with a brief note on George Rooke’s recovery from illness and customary greetings towards Barret's relatives.
mentions: Carlo Emanuele I, Duke of Savoy

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and My Very Good Lord, Your Lordship receiveth herein two papers.
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury, enclosing two intercepted papers, one of which is an original letter sent from Rome to the Jesuit Possevino. Wotton admits to having developed a keen interest in acquiring such intercepted communications, particularly those involving the Jesuits. While he does not fully identify the sender of the letter, he notes that only the first two letters of the name are visible—if they are indeed initials and not coded characters. His remarks suggest an ongoing surveillance operation targeting Catholic networks, reflecting the broader anti-Jesuit and anti-papal sentiments of English intelligence efforts during the early 17th century. The letter exemplifies Wotton’s involvement in espionage and his focus on uncovering Jesuit activities, which were viewed as subversive by the English Crown.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, Having been these four days (and so at the present) much tormented
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury, excusing himself for the shortness of his letter (caused by his illness), and briefly detailing the current situation in Venice, following the Papal interdict and its rejection by all the Venetian authorities. Wotton finishes by mentioning a few of his other messengers, which have been recently sent with other dispatches.

letters.marked: 12 of May, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: The Jesuits here finally refusing
letters.abstract: Wotton reports to the Earl of Salisbury on the final expulsion of the Jesuits from Venice following their refusal to perform ecclesiastical duties after the enforcement of the Pope’s interdict. The Venetian Senate decreed their removal, allowing them to take only their religious garments and breviaries while an official inventory of their possessions was taken. Prior to leaving, a leading Jesuit, Il Padre Barone, sought an audience with the Prince, offering Jesuit mediation between Venice and the Pope. The Prince firmly rejected the offer, asserting that Venice had never relied on such intermediaries and would not start now. Wotton describes his own role in justifying English policies against the Jesuits, refuting accusations against King James I. He highlights his speech before the Venetian Senate, where he defended England’s anti-Jesuit statutes and portrayed the Jesuits as deceptive figures manipulating public opinion. His address was well received, and the Venetian Prince reassured him of the Republic’s high regard for James I, recognizing his leadership as divinely protected. Wotton frames the Jesuits’ expulsion as a triumph against Catholic influence, reinforcing the anti-Jesuit sentiment common in early seventeenth-century Protestant diplomacy.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.marked: 19th of May, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, The differences between the Pope and State of Venice being now grown so far,
letters.abstract: Wotton reports to the Earl of Salisbury on the state of affairs in Italy following the Papal interdict of 1606, where the differences between the Pope and Venice have grown substancially. He tells of the departure  of Papal Nuncio from Venice as well as expulsion of the Venetian ambassador from Rome and mentions his two visits to Venice's Full College, which allowed him to learn of these events and judge the  actions of the Venetian State as prudent and magnificent. Finally, he expresses his hopes that this state of affairs will continue to restrict Church's control over the State matters, seeing the current situation as a confirmation of God's influence in Italy.

letters.incipit: Yesterday was the Feast of Corpus Christi,
letters.abstract: Wotton reports on the Feast of Corpus Christi in Venice, a grand event with extensive religious imagery, which he interprets as a demonstration of Venetian defiance against the Pope’s interdict. He describes the Benedictine monks’ clever workaround to avoid papal authority by using a locked chest to prevent the reception of prohibitory orders from Rome. He also notes the ongoing legal process against the Jesuits before the Council of Ten. Wotton expresses optimism that Venice may draw closer to England, not just politically but also in matters of religion. To further this, he has arranged for an Italian Protestant preacher to be sent from Geneva. The letter concludes with Wotton requesting further financial support, emphasizing that his secret intelligence efforts (particularly intercepting Jesuit communications) require substantial funding.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and My Very Good Lord, The matters here between
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice, reporting the escalating tensions between the Venetian Republic and the Papacy, which seem to be leading to war. He interprets these events as a divine reckoning meant to “purge this country.” Wotton encloses an intercepted letter from Rome, written by Lorenzo Terzo, a Jesuit who had been expelled from Venice. He vows to continue his intelligence-gathering efforts, hoping to uncover Jesuit communications between their colleges and European courts. Wotton expresses his dedication to King James I’s service and prays for Salisbury’s well-being.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I was on Tuesday last called to the College,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice, reporting his recent activities there, including several audiences in the Pien Collegio (Full College). He mentions the current situation concerning English harbours, which have since the 18th of August 1604 been open to ships from other countries, allowing foreign Princes (including the Pope), to exert their influence on the realms of King James I. Wotton announces the upcoming arrival of certain English merchants, who are meant to deliver an intercepted letter from Rome, which is too important to be sent by ordinary means. Lastly he mentions another dispatch of his (likely a letter to James I dated June 16), written in cipher and detailing other matters which are still ongoing.

letters.incipit: Here the differences between the Pope and this State
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes from Venice, reporting the deepening conflict between the Venetian Republic and the Papacy, which he believes will soon escalate into open warfare after the harvest season. The Venetian Senate has officially expelled the Jesuits from all its territories and enacted stringent legal barriers to prevent their return. The Doge, Leonardo Donato, is lauded as a resolute and highly capable leader, likened to a “Dictator of the State,” steering Venice through this crisis with political acumen and a supposed enlightenment in religious truth. In response, Rome has begun considering a formal ecclesiastical trial against Donato, though its outcome remains uncertain. Wotton hints at the wider implications of these tensions, particularly in how they may affect broader political and religious dynamics in Italy and beyond.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.marked: 14 of July, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Of the Jesuits (first dismissed and afterwards banished from hence)
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton reports to the Earl of Salisbury on the continuing conflict between Venice and the Jesuits, focusing on the case of Padre Gagliardo, a Jesuit exiled from Venice and now preaching against the Republic in Mantua. The Duke of Mantua, himself a Venetian noble, has expelled these Jesuits from his territories in defense of Venice’s honor. In response, the Venetian Senate has issued a rare public proclamation summoning Gagliardo to appear within six days or face proscription and an extraordinary bounty on his head. This decision, Wotton notes, is significant because it defies papal authority, directly opposing one of the original justifications for the Pope’s excommunication of Venice. Wotton also reports that Venice has formally warned the French ambassador, De Fresne-Canaye, to cease interceding on behalf of the Pope. The letter suggests that tensions may soon escalate into military conflict, though the likelihood of peace in Hungary and the withdrawal of Dutch forces from Spain may temper hostilities. Wotton encloses contemporary satirical epigrams and political commentary with his letter, promising further updates when events become more concrete.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice
Vincenzo I Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua

letters.marked: 21st of July, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I come this morning, being Friday
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury, informing him of a dispatch which the Venice's Pien Collegio (Full College) intends to send to the Venetian ambassador (Zorzi Giustinian) in England. He describes the letter's contents, including: thanks to king James I for his reception of the ambassador as well as his general support towards Venice, information about the ongoing troubles with the Pope (who has started to engage in military actions) following the Venetian interdict, the support that the Spanish King has shown to the Pope, as well as Venice's declaration to continue defending their independence. Wotton relates how he has communicated the king's positive attitude towards Venice and expresses his joy derived from his contribution to maintaining this diplomatic bond.

letters.marked: 18th of August, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, We had yesternight certain advertisement
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury, informing him of the tidings received recently in Venice, that the Spanish fleet has sailed to Greece and sacked Durazzo, which will likely lead to Venice being attacked in retaliation by the Ottoman Empire. Wotton also expresses his great excitement, caused not only by the turbulent state of affairs in Italy, but also by the letter he recently received from king James I, in which the monarch has conveyed his approval towards Wotton, filling him with joy and pride. Finally, Wotton promises to give in another letter an account of the fullfilment of the instructions sent from London.

letters.incipit: I send your Lordship herewith two intercepted letters
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice on August 25, 1606, enclosing two intercepted letters—one referencing Salisbury and the other Wotton himself. He expresses pride in being a target of the Jesuits’ suspicion and aligns his intelligence efforts with Salisbury’s. Wotton details his extensive spy network across key European cities (Rome, Milan, Turin, and Frankfurt), emphasizing his knowledge of Jesuit correspondence, seals, and confidants. Given the increasing costs of espionage, he requests additional secret-service funds from the Crown, citing James I’s approval of such intelligence gathering. The letter highlights the importance of espionage and interception in countering perceived Catholic threats, particularly the Jesuits, amid ongoing political and religious tensions between Venice, England, and Rome.

letters.marked: 1st of September, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I see when Kings meet,
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury, informing him of the rumours in Venice concerning the leagues which are supposedly being formed by certain European countries. Kings of England and Denmark are believed to be seeking an alliance with Venice, the States, Protestant German Princes and possibly the French king, as well as Protestants from France, Poland and Hungary. Other rumours, which Wotton deems somewhat credible, tell of Pope secretly attempting to forge a league with Spain, Emperor Rudolf II and the Italian Princes. Wotton claims that this ongoing process is the reason why the situation in Italy hasn't yet fully escalated to war, as the Pope hasn't yet secured all of his desired alliances.
mentions: Crown of the Kingdom of Poland

letters.marked: first of September, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Sacred Lord, I have received those most dear and most inestimable lines
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to king James I to thank him for a recently received letter, in which the monarch has conveyed approval towards his ambassador in Venice. Emphasizing his gratitude and the king's own virtues, Wotton shows his humble allegiance, ending the letter with the prayer for the long preservation of his Lord and Sovereign.

letters.incipit: A certain poor old man, called Benedetto Altavilla,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice on September 22, 1606, telling him of a curious event which has transpired recently in Venice. An astrologer by the name of Benedetto Altavilla visited a member of the Senate, warning him about a plan to blow up the members of Venetian nobility who were to be present the next day in the hall of the Gran Concilio. The senator has indeed found a store of gunpowder in the designated place, but the Council of Ten, instead of rewarding the astrologer, deemed him the likely culprit. However, the Vincentine has turned out to be quite resistant to torture, which some attribute to his magical powers. Currently he has been set free and continues to affirm his prophetic powers. Wotton suspects that he indeed was the one who staged the whole plot he supposedly foresaw, probably in hopes of a reward and likely taking inspiration from the recent Gunpowder Plot.

letters.marked: 22 of September, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, It seemeth very suitable and proper for me
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice on September 22, 1606, in response to his earlier dispatch from July 31. He reports on an audience in the Venetian Pien Collegio (Full College), where he represented king James I, offering support for Venice in the ongoing conflict with Pope Paul V. Wotton excuses himself for making assurances on behalf of the monarch, maintaining he only did so in service of his interests. He describes the positive response from the Doge and the College, who have also received favourable news from their own ambassador in England, Zorzi Giustinian (who has been graciously received by James I), and have in turn offered their support to the English king. Wotton concludes the letter by introducing its bearer and Wotton's own chaplain, Nathaniel Fletcher, son of Richard Fletcher, Bishop of London. Fletcher is presented as the first preacher of the Church of England beyond the Alps, who accompanied Wotton for the last two years and has personally witnessed the recent confict between Venice and the Pope, which Wotton hopes will continue idefinitely. Wotton praises Fletcher's counsel during their stay in Italy, recommending him to the list of the preachers at the English Court for the next Lent as a person wholly worthy of that honour.
mentions: Court of James VI and I
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.marked: 6th of October, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and My Very Good Lord,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury about his decision to send Rowland Woodward back to England, carrying important intelligence, including a Latin document containing the Spanish Ambassador’s opinion on the execution of Henry Garnet. Wotton expresses deep skepticism about the reliability of Jesuit narratives, after comparing the Spanish account with the testimonies of Captain Nicolas Pinner and his servant, both eyewitnesses to the execution. He finds the Spanish report, particularly concerning the alleged silence of the crowd, to be deliberately false. Wotton cynically states that he has learned from Jesuits to believe nothing from “the contrary side.” He also emphasizes that his intelligence reports hold value primarily because they pass through Salisbury’s scrutiny. Finally, Wotton attaches a letter to James I, leaving it unsealed for Salisbury’s review.

letters.incipit: My Lord, I have besides this place of my charge,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury from Venice on November 3, 1606, to ask him for an increase in his quaterly allowance. He deems it necessary for the maintaining his network of informants, as well as defrayment of personal debts. He underscores his wariness against abusing the favor of either the Secretary of State or the king, asking only for what is necessary for the fullfilment of his duties.

letters.incipit: May it please your Royal Majesty, Having here by secret means gotten the copy of a discourse
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton, writing under his alias Ottavio Baldi, informs King James I that he has obtained, through secret channels, a discourse titled I Disegni di Spagna (The Designs of Spain), allegedly written by the Doge of Venice. Wotton provides both the original and his translation, inviting James I to assess whether the argument’s strength lies in its reasoning or its rhetoric. Wotton emphasizes the political implications of the text, particularly its bearing on the balance of power in Christendom. Wotton expresses his belief that the Jesuits were the main instigators of the ongoing conflict between Venice and the Papacy, not merely as agents of the Pope or Spain, but out of their own ambition. He suggests that the Jesuits’ role was either to divert the Pope from ruling in favor of the Dominicans in their doctrinal dispute or to secure control over papal decision-making through their extensive international intelligence network. He closes by humbly seeking pardon for his candid observations, attributing them to his unwavering loyalty to James I.

letters.marked: 17 of November, 1606. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: The case of Captain William Turner is this
letters.abstract: In this letter to the Earl of Salisbury, Henry Wotton reports the arrest of Captain William Turner, an English spy who had been engaged in covert activities on behalf of the Jesuits and the Archduke Ferdinand of Styria. Turner had infiltrated Venice under the pretense of religious persecution and attempted to pass intelligence regarding English and Venetian military movements to the Archduke. His correspondence with an English Jesuit in Gratz and his attempt to destroy sensitive documents upon capture confirmed his clandestine role. Wotton, having intercepted Turner’s communications and placed him in prison, expresses his belief that the Jesuits were manipulating foreign courts for their own advantage. The letter reveals Venice’s intensified surveillance of suspected Papal and Spanish agents, reflecting the broader tensions between Venice, the Papacy, and Spain. Wotton also hints at the possibility of flipping Turner into a double agent, acknowledging that informants are often as necessary as honest men in intelligence work.
mentions: Court of Ferdinand II (Archduke of Austria and Holy Roman Emperor)

letters.incipit: May it please Your Most Excellent Majesty, Don Francesco di Castro, son to the Conde di Lemos
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton writes to king James I to inform him of the arrival of the Spanish ambassador extraordinary (Don Francesco di Castro) to Venice, as well as the course of his negotiations. He doubts whether the ambassador can achieve much in Venice and gives an analysis of the three approaches he could employ (persuasion, entreaty and menacement) in his efforts to diffuse the ongoing conflict between Rome and Venice. Wotton doesn't think that the ambassador will achieve much by means of persuasion, due to both his own flaws of character as well as the unity exhibited so far by the members of the Venetian Senate in maintaning their decrees. Similarly, it's unlikely he'd accomplish anything by means of entreaty, as such a way would be degrading for the king of Spain. Moreover, Venice isn't likely to heed the entrieties of the Spanish monarch over those of the French king, with whom they share a more amicable relationship. Finally, menacement through threats of war has already proven ineffective, as the Doge has shown a readiness to resist even military force in his speech during the public audience of the ordinary Spanish ambassador some few days prior.
mentions: Fernando Ruiz de Castro Andrade y Portugal
Francisco Gómez de Sandoval, 1st Duke of Lerma
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: I have in this interim pursued the matter of anchorage,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes to the Earl of Salisbury with reports on a few separate matters. First, he tells of his recent diplomatic efforts regarding the anchorage taxes in Venice. Having received a favourable response from the Doge, he now awaits the official resolution of the Senate. Secondly, he gives reasons for his sending of a new messenger in place of previously dispatched Rowland Woodward, who has been assailed on the road while travelling with one Sir Thomas Crompton, who perished in the attack, while Woodward was severely wounded. Papers carried by Woodward have subsequently been sent to the English ambassador in Paris, and the sensitive nature of their contents (which touch on the person of the French king Henry IV) urged Wotton to send someone to retrieve them posthaste. In the postscript, Wotton repeats information contained in that previously sent and now diverted dispatch, namely a report (given by his agent in Milan) claiming that one of the members of king James' council is feeding intelligence to the Spanish ambassador, who in turn sends it to Milan (which is under the rule of the Kingdom of Spain) and Rome. Wotton doesn't yet know the name of that collaborant, but expects to receive it in the future. He concludes the letter by stressing that such rumours without more particular details aren't in his mind sufficient for staining the reputation of one of the State's most honourable persons.
mentions: Pedro de Zúñiga y de la Cueva
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: Touching Sir Robert Dudly, I have so enormous news
letters.abstract: Writing from Venice to the Earl of Salisbury, Henry Wotton reports "enormous news" concerning Sir Robert Dudley with connection to "an honorable woman" (the news is likely related to Dudley's recent marriage to one Elizabeth Southwell, wedded in spite of the fact that Dudley already had a wife in England - Alice Dudley, Duchess of Dudley). Wotton refrains from detailing the situation in his own words, instead referring Salisbury to original accounts, which have also been sent to him. He notes how he initially considered intervening with the Grand Duke of Tuscany but abandoned this plan after learning that the Duke himself may already be implicated in the matter. He remains attentive to further developments, naming Robert Eliot (who procured a dispensation from the Pope which allowed Dudley to marry Elizabeth Southwell at Lyons) as a major participant in the whole affair. Wotton includes a short notice written by a merchant from Raguza, meant to amuse the king, and closes with a petition requesting extra financial allowances for his diplomatic service from September to December, humorously remarking on the high cost of employing even dishonest individuals in the region.

letters.incipit: In my audiences here
letters.abstract: In this letter to the Earl of Salisbury, Henry Wotton details his diplomatic stance amid the Venetian quarrel with the Pope, balancing his role between advocating for Venice’s autonomy and maintaining England’s interests. He describes his interactions with Don Francesco di Castro, emphasizing that while England and Spain are generally aligned, their representatives must act as adversaries in this particular conflict. Wotton presents himself as steadfast in reminding Venice of its sovereignty and dignity. The letter concludes with a note that a merchant’s son, traveling through France, will deliver an intercepted packet of letters from the Jesuit Robert Parsons, indicating a covert intelligence effort.

letters.incipit: Sir, I have received your last token of Spanish airs,
letters.abstract: In this letter, dated 3 February 1606 (1607 according to the new style), from Venice, Henry Wotton thanks Edward Barrett for sending a collection of Spanish musical pieces, praising one in particular while noting that the others have yet to be performed due to lacking bass parts. He comments with curiosity on their unusual lack of formal measure. Wotton mentions interest in news regarding the arrival and reception of Sir Robert Dudley and his wife in Italy. Writing in haste due to an official courier dispatch to England, he briefly addresses a request from Mr. Boughton, asking to defer his response until the next correspondence. He closes with well-wishes and greetings to Barrett’s family.

letters.marked: 16th of February, 1606⟨7⟩. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: The Cardinal Joieuse is here arrived this very day,
letters.abstract: In this letter of 16 February 1606/7, Henry Wotton reports to the Earl of Salisbury on the unexpected arrival in Venice of Cardinal Joyeuse. He notes that this development contradicts his earlier expectations, as the Cardinal has arrived before the departure of the Spanish envoy Don Francesco di Castro and seemingly with the tacit approval of the Pope. Despite indications of papal involvement, Venetian authorities officially receive Joyeuse only as the ambassador of the French king, denying him recognition as a papal legate. Wotton promises to report further on the Cardinal’s reception and mission. He reflects critically on Don Francesco’s position, suggesting that Spanish efforts have failed to gain further concessions and have actually strengthened Venetian resolve, while the French now seek to exert renewed influence through Joyeuse. Wotton affirms his own commitment to defending the principle of Venetian sovereignty in ongoing deliberations. He concludes by requesting that Salisbury inform the king of his intention to send a collection of writings related to the ongoing controversy, pending a suitable conditions for such a dispatch.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, On Friday last at evening the Cardinal Joyeuse arrived here
letters.abstract: In this letter of 23 February 1606/7, Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury of the formal arrival and ceremonious reception of Cardinal de Joyeuse in Venice as ambassador extraordinary of the French king. Wotton explains his deliberate decision not to visit the Cardinal, despite other diplomats having done so. He justifies this stance on both religious and political grounds: such a visit, even if merely ceremonial, could reflect poorly on the Protestant reputation of his sovereign, King James I, and might imply recognition of the elevated status claimed by cardinals. He further argues that acknowledging these privileges would undermine the principle of sovereignty, especially amid tensions between Venice and the Papacy. He also notes prior discourtesy from the late papal Nuncio and maintains that Joyeuse’s identity as a cardinal outweighs his diplomatic role as a French envoy. The considerations have also stopped Wotton from organizing a meeting through the ordinary French ambassador (Philippe de La Canaye). Wotton expresses frustration with the slow progress of current political affairs, which so far consist only of formalities and yield no substantive developments to report to the king. Nevertheless, he remains hopeful that divine providence will guide events to a favorable outcome. In a postscript, he thanks Salisbury for assistance shown to John Fenton, recently appointed to office in Scotland, and requests support for a Mr. Beadle (William Bedell), whom Wotton wishes to appoint as his chaplain, commending his character and abilities.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable, As I was ready to shut up this packet,
letters.abstract: In this brief letter dated 24 February 1606, Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury of intelligence received from the Doge of Venice, identifying an English merchant, Stephen Stock, based in Lucca, who is supplying gunpowder and munitions to the Pope. Wotton leaves it to the judgment of king James to take appropriate actions against Stock and others similarly offering support to papal forces. He also requests that Salisbury communicate this matter to the Venetian ambassador (Zorzi Giustinian), noting that the information originates from the Duke (likely meaning the Grand Duke of Tuscany, Ferdinando I de’ Medici, given Lucca's placement in Tuscany).

letters.incipit: May it please Your Most Excellent Majesty, I received by the last post a form or rule under your Royal hand,
letters.abstract: In this letter of 9 March 1607, Henry Wotton (writing under the name Ottavio Baldi) reports to King James I on a recent exchange with the French ambassador regarding a proposed Anglo-French cooperation. Acting under the king’s instructions, Wotton recounts how he restated the ambassador’s earlier proposal while emphasizing the need for a clear and suitable foundation before entering into any formal agreement, particularly if the French king’s name were not explicitly involved. The French ambassador responds by clarifying that his original intent had been to promote joint support by England and France for the Dutch States, then under severe pressure from the Spanish. He suggests that Wotton misunderstood his earlier remarks and expresses concern that England appears reluctant to assist, citing reports that James I had recently sought repayment of loans previously granted by Queen Elizabeth to the States and the French king, despite their ongoing financial burdens in resisting Spain. Nevertheless, the ambassador indicates willingness to advance negotiations if assured of king James’s commitment, offering to facilitate contact with French official Baron de Rosny and promising the French monarch's cooperation. Wotton acknowledged the initial misunderstanding and concludes by affirming his loyal service, invoking divine protection for the king and for Venice amid its ongoing political and religious tensions.
mentions: Maximilien de Béthune, duc de Sully

letters.marked: 6th of April, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: As I advertised his Majesty by the last post,
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury of the near resolution of the crisis between Venice and the Papacy, with an outcome that he sees as favorable to Venice and to Protestant interests. He recounts a speech he delivered before the Venetian College, in which he praised King James I for his support, asserting that his intervention was crucial to securing Venice’s autonomy in the dispute. Wotton highlights that the Venetian Republic will not use terms such as “rebenediction” or “absolution” to describe the agreement, preferring instead accomodamento (settlement), which maintains their sovereignty. He further notes that the resolution will include a permanent exclusion of the Jesuits from Venetian territories, despite prior efforts to reinstate them. Wotton emphasizes Venice’s deep gratitude to James I and its commitment to preserving its jurisdiction against any future Papal pressures. The letter underscores the complex political maneuvers at play, with France and Spain also actively involved in shaping the final agreement.

letters.marked: 18th of May, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Having formerly given your Lordship a general accompt
letters.abstract: This letter from Henry Wotton to Sir Thomas Edmondes, dated May 18, 1607, provides a detailed account of the resolution of the Venetian conflict with the Papacy. Wotton outlines the specific terms of the agreement, which include the revocation of the Pope’s interdict, the conditional return of certain religious orders (excluding the Jesuits), and the extradition of two ecclesiastical prisoners to Rome at the request of the French King. He notes the strategic ambiguity in the language used by both sides, particularly regarding the Pope’s authority, hinting at unresolved tensions. Wotton also highlights the Venetian Senate’s decision to grant lifelong protection and pensions to the intellectual defenders of the Republic, emphasizing the ongoing ideological battle. He describes how the Cardinal de Joyeuse formally revoked the interdict under French auspices, yet Venice minimized any public recognition of this papal act, reinforcing its stance of maintaining full sovereignty. The letter concludes with Wotton’s reflection on the subtle diplomatic maneuvering and his expectation that tensions would persist, albeit in a less overt form.

letters.abstract: In this letter to the Earl of Salisbury, dated June 22, 1607, Henry Wotton reports on the growing momentum of religious reform in Venice following its recent conflict with the Papacy. He notes that the Venetian state takes pride in its resolution of tensions with the Pope and anticipates a diplomatic response from King James I. Wotton expresses confidence that the Protestant cause is advancing in Venice, attributing this progress to the writings and private teachings of Maestro Paolo Sarpi and his associates. He draws a parallel between Sarpi’s efforts and the work of St. Paul in Corinth, emphasizing both the challenges and the potential for transformation in a city known for its moral laxity. Wotton closes by reaffirming his loyalty and service to Salisbury.

letters.marked: 3rd of August, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Your Lordship's of the 11th of July
letters.abstract: This letter from Henry Wotton to Sir Thomas Edmondes discusses two key issues: the political-religious tensions in the Grisons and the conversion of Tobie Matthew to Catholicism. Wotton reports on the ongoing struggle between the Grisons and the Spanish, highlighting Count Fuentes’ attempt to frame the conflict as a religious persecution to rally Catholic allies. He also mentions the fear that Archduke Maximilian of Tyrol may intervene, exacerbating tensions. Additionally, Wotton expresses disappointment at the conversion of Tobie Matthew, son of the Archbishop of York, lamenting the potential influence of Jesuits in exploiting his apostasy. The letter reflects Wotton’s concern for the Protestant cause in Europe and his broader intelligence-gathering efforts.

letters.marked: 13th of September, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Your Lordship receiveth by this gentleman the books
letters.abstract: In this letter of 13 September 1607, Henry Wotton, ambassador in Venice, writes to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, sending recently published books on the 1606–1607 papal–Venetian dispute and a private portrait of the Servite friar Paolo Sarpi. Wotton describes Sarpi as a secretly Protestant-leaning figure of deep learning, critical of papal authority, and well-regarded by the Venetian Senate. He urges Salisbury to secure a copy of the Pope’s breve against King James’s oath of allegiance—Sarpi intends to show it to the Senate as proof that Rome seeks to dissolve the sovereignty of princes. Wotton highlights the strategic importance of Sarpi’s covert collaboration with his own chaplain for “less observation” of their activities. He closes by commending a trusted messenger to Salisbury’s favor and requesting the breve be forwarded swiftly.

letters.marked: 2d of October, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: I am moved to set down among these things, the steps of an imperfect business
Having lately troubled your Lordship
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton writes from Venice on 12 October 1607 to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, reporting on the recent attempted assassination of the Venetian theologian Paolo Sarpi. He encloses the formal sentence passed by the Venetian Council of Ten on the offenders and describes the widespread outrage, including the Venetian government’s intense pursuit of the culprits and its special care for Sarpi’s recovery. Wotton highlights the political ramifications, including suspicions that Rome—the Pope or his agents—was behind the attack. He also notes that the Papal Nuncio in Venice is in both physical and mental distress, possibly from fear of repercussions. Wotton concludes with an update on Sarpi’s condition and reflects on the event as an instance of “God’s miraculous Providence.”

letters.marked: the first of November, 1607. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: For the course of things in this place
letters.abstract: Sir Henry Wotton, the English ambassador to Venice, updates Robert Cecil (the Earl of Salisbury) on the aftermath of the attempted assassination of Fra Paolo Sarpi. In Letter 113 (1 November 1607), Wotton reports Sarpi’s near recovery and notes that both the Council of Ten and the Venetian Senate are publicly reaffirming their protection of him. Wotton names three fugitive suspects—“Poma, the priest, and the Florentine”—last sighted traveling through Ancona and arriving in Rome armed with prohibited weapons, implying papal collusion. The Venetian ambassador in Rome has been instructed to spare no expense to uncover who orchestrated the attack.

letters.abstract: This letter provides a snapshot of Venetian politics in early 1607, showcasing Wotton’s continued engagement in espionage and diplomatic maneuvering. The harsh sentencing of Angelo Badoero highlights Venice’s strict control over internal affairs, while Wotton’s depiction of Archduke Ferdinand as a Jesuit puppet aligns with broader English fears of Catholic influence. The dramatic account of Sir Julius Caesar’s son’s death adds an element of personal tragedy, linking the diplomatic narrative to English interests. Wotton’s conspiratorial mindset remains evident in his framing of events. He portrays the Jesuits as omnipresent manipulators, the Papal Nuncio as a scheming but ineffective agent, and Venice as heroically resisting foreign encroachment. His letter serves both as intelligence and as a piece of rhetorical persuasion, reinforcing England’s perception of Catholic powers as inherently conspiratorial.

Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I will only this week entertain his Majesty with the enclosed paper.
Having at the present sufficiently troubled your Lordship
letters.abstract: Writing from Venice on 28 March 1608, Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury that King James I’s Apologia pro Iuramento Fidelitatis (a defense of the Oath of Allegiance) has arrived and circulated among Venetian leadership. Even before Wotton could present a copy to the Doge formally, the Doge had already received one from England and consulted with a “party” (almost certainly Paolo Sarpi). The book has sparked discussion among “residents and other instruments of state.” Wotton requests more copies of the Apologia and additional Protestant works (referencing a catalog Salisbury sent), hoping to distribute them in Venice for “a great many” who might be receptive. In particular, he wants small–format editions of Bishop John Jewel’s Apology, well–suited for discreet circulation and influencing Venetian opinion. Wotton closes by noting a brewing conflict in Austria between Emperor Rudolf II and his brother Archduke Matthias, stemming from a dispute over religious freedom in Hungary and adjacent regions.

Such particulars as I hear from Rome touching Tirone
letters.abstract: This letter, dated from Venice in May (?), 1608, relays intelligence from Rome concerning Tyrone’s activities. According to the report, Tyrone—accompanied largely by the Primate of Ireland—visited various cardinals and ambassadors. From Cardinals Farnese and Mont’ Alto he received favorable words. In Rome, among a group dispatched from the English College (including Thomas Fitzharbert and John Sweete), he was noted for his interaction with English exiles. Notably, upon seeing Sir Anthony Standen, he is reputed to have declared that “it is better being poor in Rome than rich in prison in England.” Furthermore, the letter details two private audiences with the Pope, mentions his lodging in a palace alongside the Persian ambassador and Sir Anthony Sherly, and reports that the Pope intends to limit his board to twelve persons amid rising discontent. Rumors include a pension of ten thousand crowns per annum from the King of Spain for the support of the Irish, along with scattered personal observations regarding Tyrone’s wife. Overall, the letter interweaves documented diplomatic encounters with rumor, reflecting the intricate network of political, religious, and personal intrigues among exiled English and Irish figures in Rome.

Having both extraordinary occasion and a fit opportunity
letters.abstract: In this letter, Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury about a significant defection in Venice: Monsignor Ribetta, the vicar of the Patriarch, has fled to Rome under the influence of the Patriarch himself, who is allegedly seeking a cardinalship. The Senate reacts to this betrayal by curbing the Patriarch’s financial privileges rather than taking harsher measures. Wotton draws a parallel to Henry VIII’s dissolution of monasteries, suggesting that this restriction will prevent the return of the Jesuits. He also expresses gratitude for Salisbury’s support of his countryman, John Finett, and concludes with a reference to his own unprofitability in service.

letters.incipit: From Rome we hear that Poma
letters.abstract: In this dispatch of fifth December 1608 from Venice, Sir Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury that Ridolfo Poma, implicated in the failed attempt on Fra Paolo Sarpi’s life, now enjoys guarded favor in Rome, causing the Pope an awkward dilemma between leniency and exposing the Church’s role in sponsoring assassins. Wotton further reveals two new conspiracies uncovered against Sarpi, including one hatched by his own “converse” and relatives from Viterbo. Meanwhile, Lord Roos has arrived in Venice and fallen ill, yet demonstrates a resolute aversion to Catholicism. Finally, Wotton outlines a covert plan to free the imprisoned Mr. Mole by funneling funds through Nicholas Fitzherbert, who hopes to regain King James’s favor.

letters.incipit: My very good Lord, I have of late received weekly from your Lordship very kind information of such things as occur with you there,
My Lord, I have this week received your Lordship’s last of the 17th of December.

letters.marked: 16th of January, 1608⟨9⟩. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: The presenter hereof (by name Francesco Biondi)
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton introduces Giovanni Francesco Biondi to King James I, describing him as a learned and devout man from Dalmatia who has sought refuge in England to practice his religion more freely. Biondi had previously served as secretary to Cavaliere Pietro Priuli, the Venetian ambassador to France, and had maintained contact with English agents, notably Sir George Carew. Biondi had risked his life to transport a Protestant nobleman’s library from France to Venice and had maintained ties with Reformed Churches in the Grisons, Geneva, and France. Based on these qualities, Wotton recommends him to James I. Additionally, Maestro Paulo (Paolo Sarpi), a key Venetian reformer and anti-papal thinker, entrusts Biondi to deliver certain proposals to the English monarch for broader religious and political purposes. Wotton underscores Biondi’s integrity and loyalty to Protestant causes, asking the King to receive him favorably.

letters.incipit: Being most assured that I shall yield your Majesty
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton reports to James I about the preaching of Fra Fulgenzio Micanzio, a Venetian Servite friar, who delivers sermons at St. Lorenzo promoting Protestant-leaning theology. His preaching, which emphasizes scriptural authority over papal doctrine, has drawn large audiences, including many Venetian senators and gentlemen. The Inquisition attempted to silence Micanzio, but the Duke of Venice protected him. The Venetian Senate, in response to the papal opposition, doubled the salaries of their state-sponsored theologians and reaffirmed their commitment to religious independence from Rome. Wotton also recounts a humorous episode involving a Venetian noblewoman, a Mocenigo, who bequeathed 10,000 crowns to the Jesuits, but with the condition that they could only receive it upon their return to Venice. Given the Venetian state’s expulsion of the Jesuits, this effectively ensured they would never reclaim the money, inadvertently strengthening Venice’s stance against the Jesuits.

letters.incipit: May it please your Honour, It hath not been (as I can truly profess) any want of duty towards your honourable person,

letters.marked: 24th of April, 1609. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: The resident ambassador of the Signory at Rome
letters.abstract: This letter reports the reaction of Pope Paul V to the preaching of Fra Fulgenzio Micanzio, which had stirred controversy in Venice. The Venetian ambassador in Rome informed the Duke of Venice that the Pope, after hearing complaints from Cardinal Lanfranco, angrily denounced Fulgenzio’s sermons, asserting that preaching the pure Gospel and Scripture amounted to an attack on the Catholic faith. The Venetian Senate, upon hearing this remark, reacted with murmurs and scandal, perceiving the Pope’s words as proof of the Church’s suppression of biblical teaching. Paolo Sarpi (Padre Paulo), a leading Venetian theologian, saw this as a key moment in exposing Rome’s hostility toward religious reform, believing it would help open the eyes of the Venetian authorities to papal overreach. This letter underscores the widening rift between Venice and Rome, highlighting the Venetian desire for religious independence and the increasing tension over Protestant-leaning reforms within the Republic.

letters.marked: 24th of April, 1609. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I will present unto his Majesty no other occurrence by this post
They have here within these two days
letters.abstract: In this letter from Venice, Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury about recent events concerning the punishment of friars. A friar who had been exiled for aiding secret communications between the Papal Nuncio and Angelo Badoero was caught returning and sentenced to ten years of imprisonment. Another monk from Perugia, allegedly involved in a plot to assassinate Maestro Paulo (Paolo Sarpi), was executed in secrecy by the Venetian Council of Ten. Wotton notes that while these occurrences may seem minor compared to the affairs of other English agents abroad, he believes they signal larger developments in Venice. He then requests a brief hiatus in his correspondence, citing medical advice to visit the Baths of Abano for treatment of a suspected kidney or bladder ailment.

letters.incipit: A remembrance for your Lordship’s secretary that it may please his Lordship hereafter
Postscript. — Before the departure of this bearer
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton relays Maestro Paolo (Paolo Sarpi)’s suggestion that England mediate between the Dutch Republic and Venice by encouraging the former to report on their treaty negotiations, subtly fostering closer ties without Venice appearing to seek them directly. Sarpi argues that England, as the “balancer of Christendom,” is best positioned for such a role, allowing Venice to maintain a posture of passive prudence while still benefiting from the alliance. Wotton questions why Venice does not initiate this exchange through its own ambassador in England, but Sarpi insists that Venetian diplomacy prefers indirect engagement. The proposal extends to Brandenburg’s claim to Cleves, recognizing shifting German alliances as another diplomatic opportunity. Wotton closes by noting that Giovanni Francesco Biondi, if still in England, could prepare the ground for these negotiations as part of his upcoming travels. The letter reflects the covert nature of early modern diplomacy, where states maneuvered carefully to advance their interests while maintaining strategic discretion.

letters.incipit: About the time of this bearer's departure,
letters.abstract: In this letter, Wotton expresses deep concern over the systematic targeting of English Protestant travelers in Catholic Europe, particularly their tutors, whom he claims are being deliberately separated from their students by Jesuit-influenced authorities. He recounts the arrest of Edward Lichefeld by Dominican friars and his imprisonment by the Inquisition, paralleling it with similar cases, including that of Mr. Mole in Rome. Wotton portrays the Jesuits as covert manipulators within the Papal court, orchestrating intelligence operations to preemptively monitor and influence English noblemen before they arrive in Rome. His language reflects both real geopolitical tensions and conspiratorial anxieties, particularly regarding the supposed “reconciliation” of Lichefeld within the Jesuit novitiate, which he suspects to be a strategic fabrication. He highlights the broader trend of religious surveillance and coercion, linking these events to a calculated strategy aimed at undermining Protestant influence in the region. Throughout, Wotton grapples with uncertainty, admitting his growing difficulty in distinguishing reality from deception, reinforcing his broader narrative of Catholic intrigue.

letters.marked: Last of July, 1609. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: This worthy Duke,
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton describes his formal presentation of King James I’s book to the Doge of Venice, framing the occasion as an auspicious event occurring on St. James’s Day. Wotton elaborates on the significance of monarchs engaging in writing, reinforcing James’s literary work as a testament to his wisdom and leadership. He draws a direct connection between the book and England’s stance on sovereignty, particularly in response to the Papal influence, likening the Pope’s interference in secular affairs to the uncontrollable flooding of the Tiber. Wotton highlights his own role in ensuring that the Doge correctly understands James’s intent—not to interfere with Venetian governance but to assert the necessity of resistance against Papal overreach. The letter reflects Wotton’s diplomatic tact, emphasizing the importance of Venice’s recognition of James’s support while securing Venetian goodwill in the broader Protestant-Catholic struggle.

letters.marked: 14th of August, 1609. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: I have now by secret means gotten a copy of that censure
letters.abstract: In this letter of 14 August 1609, Henry Wotton (signing himself as “Ottavio Baldi”) writes to King James I from Venice. He reports that the Pope has issued a “censure” against the King’s recently published book—one that defends the English Oath of Allegiance and clarifies James’s religious stance. The Pope personally gave a copy of this condemnation to the Venetian ambassador’s secretary, intending to prevent Venice from receiving James’s “blessed labours.” Wotton relays that covert demand for King James’s book is high, and many in Venice secretly desire copies. Wotton’s chaplain has translated the King’s work into Italian, seeking input from Fra Paolo Sarpi and Fulgenzio Micanzio. Both friars admire James’s confessional summary and see him as especially suited, “above all [his] predecessors,” to extend true religion not just in Europe but also in America (“Nova Britannia”). Meanwhile, Wotton thanks the King for letting him remain longer in Venice before returning to England. The postscript adds that the Grand Duke of Tuscany has burned James’s book under the Inquisition’s direction, the Spanish ambassador claims the Duke of Savoy rejected it, and in Rome it was publicly banned and equated with Beza’s Confessions. Yet Wotton suggests that such prohibitions only heighten curiosity among curious Venetians.

letters.marked: 14th of August, 1609. Style of the place.
letters.incipit: My Lord, I have, by your Lordship’s letter of this week,
My Lord, I have addressed unto your Lordship three bills,
It may please his Majesty to be informed that,
letters.abstract: In this letter, Henry Wotton informs the Earl of Salisbury about the prohibition of King James I’s book, Apologia pro iureamento fidelitatis, in Venice. He attributes the censorship to the Papal Nuncio, who allegedly took advantage of the Doge’s illness to secure the Venetian College’s approval for the ban. Wotton expresses both skepticism and frustration, noting that while the prohibition was issued, it did not explicitly name James I as the author, nor did it impose penalties on booksellers. He employs an informant, Francesco Biondi, to investigate, revealing that copies are expected from Basel, and that a prominent bookseller, Giambattista Ciotti, remains willing to supply them. Wotton characterizes Ciotti as “Jesuitical,” reinforcing his anti-Jesuit conspiratorial lens. He resolves to publicly protest the prohibition and promises a detailed report to James I in his next letter. The letter blends genuine diplomatic concerns with Wotton’s conspiratorial interpretation of Catholic influence in Venice.

letters.marked: the 18th of September, 1609. Style of the place
letters.incipit: Albeit at the first I inclined (as I must confess) to resolve the matter into irrision,
letters.abstract: Wotton reports in detail his diplomatic intervention regarding the prohibition in Venice of King James I's book (Premonition to All Most Mighty Monarchs). After learning that the prohibition had been imposed without Senate approval and that several Venetian senators expected him to complain publicly, he formally protested before the Venetian authorities. He first requested that the ban be lifted and stressed that the prohibition constituted an affront to King James's friendship towards Venice. After receiving no satisfactory response, he demanded either the punishment of the Inquisitor responsible or a public demonstration of Venetian respect for the King. Dissatisfied with the Senate's final resolution, Wotton declared that he would cease to act publicly as ambassador until King James specified his further instructions. The letter also refers to the scandal surrounding an anti-Jacobean libel that had circulated from the Venetian ambassador's household in England.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice
