letters.marked: the 2d of October. Style of the place, 1609
letters.incipit: I cannot forbear to signify unto his Majesty that at this audience,
letters.abstract: Following an audience before the Venetian Collegio, Wotton reports an unusual political incident connected with the recent appointment of a special Venetian ambassador to England [Francesco Contarini, says Smith]. As he began referring to his own earlier complaint while praising the newly appointed ambassador, several members of the Collegio identified as Papalini abruptly left the chamber. Wotton interprets their withdrawal as evidence that individuals with close familial ties to the Roman Church should not participate in deliberations concerning papal affairs. He notes in particular the embarrassed reaction of Giorgio Giustiniani, nephew of the Bishop of Padua, and argues that these men had previously remained in the Collegio only through unofficial tolerance rather than by right.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: May it please your most excellent Majesty, I am advertised from Rome by assured means
letters.abstract: Wotton reports intelligence received from Rome concerning Pope Paul V's reaction to King James's recent book. According to a reliable source, the Pope publicly remarked that the King had "lost his mind," since the publication now gave him sufficient grounds to excommunicate him without issuing a prior warning (monitorio). Rumours of a possible papal excommunication subsequently circulate in Venice, prompting a diplomat representing the Dukes of Modena and Bavaria to inquire about Wotton's opinion. Rather than responding directly, Wotton recounts that he answered by posing four rhetorical questions: whether Paul V was more formidable than Pius V; whether James I was a lesser sovereign than Elizabeth I; whether excommunications retained the same authority they once had; and whether, after excommunicating the King, the Jesuits possessed any more dangerous weapon than the Gunpowder Plot. Wotton concludes by minimizing the entire issue, describing it as scarcely more significant than "Garnet's straw," and refers the King to the report sent separately to the Lord Treasurer regarding current Venetian affairs.
mentions: Dutch gentleman|Cesare d'Este, Duke of Modena
Gregorio Barbarigo|Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria

letters.incipit: At the present I have nothing to signify but the arrival here this day of an ambassador from the States
letters.abstract: Wotton informs Cecil of the arrival in Venice of the ambassador of the Dutch Republic, Cornelius Vandermyle, sent to announce the conclusion of the Twelve Years' Truce and to strengthen diplomatic relations with Venice. Wotton extends him diplomatic assistance and guidance regarding ceremonial protocol, as his arrival has aroused suspicion among pro-Spanish and pro-papal circles, where rumours circulate that his mission aims to negotiate an alliance against the Pope and the King of Spain. He further reports on diplomatic developments concerning Hugh O'Neill (Earl of Tyrone), communications between the Count of Fuentes and Edward Stanley, and the mission of Sir Robert Sherley, ambassador of the Shah of Persia, accompanied by Tobie Mathew. Sherley seeks to encourage the Christian powers to continue the war against the Ottoman Empire. Wotton concludes with a personal reflection on Emperor Rudolf II, portraying him as an ineffective ruler whose excessive submission to the papacy has, in his view, been providentially punished by the loss of obedience among his own subjects.
mentions: Pedro Henriquez de Acevedo, Count of Fuentes
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: Postscript: My Lord, I received some while since a letter from your Lordship by Mr. William Litton
letters.abstract: In a brief postscript, Wotton informs Robert Cecil that he has received his letter through the young William Lytton. He praises Lytton's character, diligence, and intellectual curiosity, expressing confidence that his travels in Italy will broaden his knowledge and benefit him upon his return to England. Wotton reports that Lytton is currently studying in Padua and assures Cecil that he considers it an honour to assist him, in accordance with his request.

letters.incipit: May it please your most excellent Majesty, This day being the New Year’s Eve with us here
letters.abstract: Wotton writes to James I to express gratitude for the King's support following complaints made against him by the Venetian government concerning his conduct over the circulation and prohibition of the King's book. Having learned through the Earl of Salisbury that James had defended him before the Venetian ambassador, Wotton thanks the King for his gracious intervention. He then offers a sincere apology for the excessive zeal ("the immoderation of my proceeding") with which he handled the affair, acknowledging that his actions resulted from errors of judgement rather than ill intent. He concludes by asking for the King's forgiveness and offering New Year wishes together with renewed professions of loyalty.

letters.incipit: I was taking the air in my gondola
letters.abstract: Wotton reports an incident that occurred while he was travelling by gondola in Venice. Having stopped to inquire about an English galley slave whom he believed to be unjustly detained, he witnessed the Greek commander of the galley, Piero Scordili, violently strike the prisoner and then insult and threaten Wotton himself. Wotton immediately lodged a formal complaint with the Venetian authorities. The Venetian College and Senate reacted swiftly, imprisoning Scordili and sentencing him to perpetual imprisonment in order to uphold the honour of the English ambassador. The English prisoner was released from the galley and relieved of minor debts. Wotton remarks, however, that the Venetian authorities punished the captain so severely that he later found himself petitioning for his release out of compassion for his family, stressing that his original complaint had been motivated solely by concern for diplomatic honour rather than personal resentment.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: May it please your Highness, Beside that which I have now represented unto your Highness

letters.marked: the 21th of January 1609⟨10⟩. Style of the place
letters.incipit: May it please your most Excellent Majesty, I present herein unto your Majesty
letters.abstract: This letter, written by Sir Henry Wotton to King James I on January 21, 1610, describes how Henry IV of France attempted to undermine Protestant activities in Venice by using an intercepted letter to expose covert Protestant networks. Giovanni Diodati, an Italian Protestant theologian from Geneva, had written to a French official about Protestant affairs in Venice. Somehow, the letter fell into the hands of the Jesuit Father Pierre Cotton, Henry IV’s confessor, who then showed it to the French king. Henry IV forwarded copies to the Pope and the French ambassador in Venice, who delayed its presentation for strategic reasons, possibly waiting for Papalist factions in the Venetian Senate to prepare the ground. Wotton interprets these actions as part of a broader French effort to curry favor with Rome, possibly as preparation for a future alliance or to facilitate the return of the Jesuits to Venice. Wotton also notes a subtle but significant pressure campaign directed at Paolo Sarpi, urging him to seek papal absolution. The letter reflects England’s diplomatic interest in countering Catholic influence in Venice and maintaining its Protestant allies.
mentions: Carlo Emanuele I, Duke of Savoy
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.marked: the 29th of January, 1609⟨10⟩. Style of the place
letters.incipit: Before I end, I must not forget again to render your Lordship very humble thanks for your last
letters.abstract: Wotton thanks the Earl of Salisbury for a recent letter, which reassured him of Salisbury's continued favour following an earlier communication concerning a more troubling matter. Acknowledging his own indiscretion, Wotton expresses gratitude that Salisbury has not withdrawn his support and reaffirms his unwavering loyalty and devotion. He concludes by expressing his hope of demonstrating his gratitude and sincerity in person.

letters.incipit: Sir, I have been desirous of some fit opportunity
letters.abstract: Wotton thanks Sir Arthur Throckmorton for a previous friendly letter and sends his reply through Nicholas Bacon, who is returning to England. Reflecting on his own career, Wotton modestly describes himself primarily as "a poor scholar," insisting that scholarship, rather than diplomacy, represents his true vocation and highest ambition. He characterizes his diplomatic office as an honour bestowed by James I rather than a role naturally suited to his character, claiming that he is better fitted to serve truth than political artifice. He briefly reports that Italy is currently peaceful, although concerns remain over the ambitious designs of Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy, whose aspirations are likely to receive encouragement from foreign powers. He concludes by sending his regards to Throckmorton's wife, daughters, and household, acknowledging the family connection created through marriage.
mentions: Carlo Emanuele I, Duke of Savoy

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, The time drawing now onwards apace which his Majesty hath prefixed for my return
letters.abstract: As the date fixed by James I for his return from Venice approaches, Wotton asks the Earl of Salisbury to support his request for a new diplomatic assignment among the Protestant princes of Germany on his journey home. He argues that, having acquired first-hand knowledge of Venetian affairs, he would be well placed to encourage greater cooperation between the German Protestant rulers and England in advancing the Protestant cause. He presents the proposal modestly, stressing his loyalty and zeal while leaving Salisbury free to suppress the request if he judges it inappropriate. Pending the King's decision, Wotton promises to continue gathering observations on the political character, customs, and objectives of the Venetian Republic, whose policies he describes as exceptionally changeable and shaped by its maritime environment. He concludes by refraining from discussing public affairs further in order to focus on his personal request.

letters.incipit: The matter touching D i o d a t i is almost forgotten
letters.abstract: Wotton reports that the controversy surrounding Diodati's intercepted correspondence has largely subsided and should not be revived. He offers an assessment of the political climate in Venice, noting that the Great Council is generally favourable to patriotic and Protestant interests, whereas the Collegio is particularly unfavourable at present. He comments on the postponement of his return to England and requests that his period of service might be slightly shortened for practical reasons. Most notably, he informs Salisbury and James I of Galileo Galilei's newly published Sidereus Nuncius, describing the discovery of Jupiter's four satellites, the nature of the Milky Way, the irregular surface of the Moon, and the implications of these discoveries for astronomy and astrology. Finally, Wotton discusses rumours of a planned Franco-Savoyard attack on the Duchy of Milan and reports French diplomatic efforts to strengthen relations with Venice, while expressing concern that foreign military intervention in Italy might encourage closer relations between Venice and the Papacy.
mentions: Carlo Emanuele I, Duke of Savoy
Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.incipit: My Lord, That small service which your Lordship left in my hands
letters.abstract: Wotton informs the recipient that the Pope, through Don Francesco di Castro and the Spanish ambassador, has agreed to guarantee his safety should he visit Rome, provided that his stay is brief and his behaviour causes no public scandal. Wotton strongly advises against accepting the offer, arguing that the papal guarantee is unreliable and could easily be withdrawn or manipulated. He warns that the recipient would be closely monitored in Rome and cites the recent case of Fulgenzio Manfredi, who was arrested by the Roman Inquisition despite having received a safe-conduct. Wotton recommends abandoning the journey altogether and openly stating that he does not trust the Pope.
mentions: Alfonso de la Cueva-Benavides y Mendoza-Carrillo

letters.incipit: Mr. Nicholas Bacon, and my servant Harry Cogan
letters.abstract: Wotton acknowledges Salisbury's continued support following the decision to postpone his return to England until the following autumn. Referring to messages conveyed by Nicholas Bacon and his servant Harry Cogan, he thanks Salisbury for his favourable remarks concerning the extension of his diplomatic appointment. While admitting his natural desire to return home, Wotton recognises the importance of remaining in royal service and expresses gratitude for both King James I's continued confidence and Salisbury's patronage. He concludes by reporting that the Venetian authorities have warmly welcomed the King's recent demonstrations of goodwill, communicated in advance by the extraordinary ambassador's arrival.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, On Saturday last about noon, arrived here an extraordinary dispatch
letters.abstract: Wotton reports that news of the assassination of Henry IV of France has reached Venice through successive dispatches from the Venetian ambassadors in Savoy and France. Initially, the Venetian Senate hesitated to believe the report, suspecting it might be Spanish disinformation intended to influence military preparations. Confirmation soon arrived from the Venetian ambassador in France, causing widespread political anxiety in Venice. Wotton discusses the likely diplomatic consequences of Henry IV's death, particularly the strengthening of the alliance between the Papacy, the Habsburg Empire, and Spain in the dispute over the Duchy of Cleves, while casting doubt on the future ambitions of the Duke of Savoy. He concludes with a strongly confessional reflection, interpreting Henry IV's assassination as divine judgement. Wotton emphasizes that the king died without receiving the Catholic sacraments and argues that the doctrine responsible for encouraging regicide belonged not to Protestantism but to Roman Catholicism, alluding particularly to Jesuit teachings. He closes with prayers for the protection of James I from similar threats.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, Being this week in a villa, some two or three miles out of Venice
letters.abstract: Wotton reports that Venice was briefly thrown into confusion by a false rumour, originating from letters sent by Flemish merchants from Antwerp, claiming that James I had been shot in the shoulder by a carpenter or joiner working at court. While staying at his villa outside Venice, Wotton learned that Venetian authorities had immediately sought confirmation of the King's condition and expressed sincere concern for his safety. Venetian diplomatic correspondence from London and The Hague contained no mention of such an event, leading the Venetian government to conclude that the report was maliciously fabricated, possibly inspired by the recent assassination of Henry IV of France. Wotton uses the incident to emphasize both James I's popularity in Venice and divine protection over the King.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, It will be strange to tell his Majesty (though very true)
letters.abstract: Wotton reports that, contrary to expectations following the assassination of Henry IV of France, political anxieties in Venice have increased, particularly regarding the ambitions of the Duke of Savoy. He describes the Duke as deeply dissatisfied with his political situation due to Spanish influence within his territories and notes that he has recently sought the advice and assistance of the Venetian Republic through his ambassador. Wotton further observes that the French ambassador soon afterwards appeared to support Savoy's objectives, suggesting newly received instructions from France. He concludes with his own assessment that the Duke of Savoy cannot remain politically neutral: he must ultimately align either with France or Spain, and whichever course he chooses is likely to generate conflict with the other power.
mentions: Carlo Emanuele I, Duke of Savoy

letters.marked: this 29 of July, 1610. Style of the place
letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, It hath pleased the Lord my God to deliver me of a painful fever
letters.abstract: Wotton informs Cecil that he has survived a severe fever contracted during the exceptionally hot Venetian summer. After three weeks of illness, which left him weaker than a previous prolonged infirmity, this is the first day on which he feels relief from pain and sufficient strength to dictate a letter. He thanks Salisbury for his concern and support during his illness and expresses the hope of resuming his ordinary diplomatic correspondence with King James in the next dispatch. He concludes by noting that political affairs in Venice remain somewhat ambiguous.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable and my very good Lord, I can truly say that your Lordship’s last of the 4th of July
letters.abstract: Having substantially recovered from his recent illness, Wotton thanks Cecil for his letter of 4 July, which restored his spirits and gave him renewed strength. He expresses particular gratitude for being informed that he is expected to be relieved of his Venetian embassy early November. Wotton welcomes this prospect, stating that, should it accord with King James's wishes, he longs to lay aside the office of ambassador, which he feels does not suit his true nature, and to return to Cecil in the simplicity and sincerity that he professes. Finally, he reassures him that neither he nor his household fear travelling during the autumn or early winter, remarking that no season can be unpleasant when one is travelling home. He concludes with the Italian proverb "uccelli di bosco et di riviera", suggesting that after experiencing many different climates they are now accustomed to every kind of weather.

letters.incipit: Not long since a gentleman of some forty years
letters.abstract: Henry Wotton reports to the Earl of Salisbury about a dubious French informant, Claudio de’ Giuberti, who claims to have uncovered a plot against King James I in Rome. The informant, allegedly trained at the Papal Court, describes an Englishman seeking revenge for religious persecution, supposedly carrying a stiletto as proof of his intent. Wotton, skeptical of the informant’s credibility, confirms with the French ambassador that he was a known opportunist seeking financial reward. Additionally, Wotton discusses the trial and execution of Fra Fulgenzio Manfredi in Rome, noting that false accusations were made against him regarding correspondence with King James and the English ambassador. Wotton publicly refutes these charges, leading to a strong reaction in the Venetian Senate, reinforcing his role in defending England’s interests.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.abstract: Henry Wotton provides the Marquis of Buckingham with a detailed account of the deaths of the Venetian doges Giovanni Bembo and Niccolò Donato, together with the successive elections of their successors. He begins with an obituary of Bembo, reviewing his military and political career, personal character, and conduct as doge, before describing the constitutional procedures following a doge's death, including the appointment of Correctors and Inquisitors and the introduction of electoral reforms. Wotton then analyses the principal candidates in the ensuing election—Antonio Priuli, Girolamo Giustiniani, Agostino Nani, and Niccolò Donato—assessing their political reputations, familial alliances, strengths, and liabilities. He offers a detailed explanation of the complex Venetian electoral process and the shifting alliances among the forty-one electors that resulted in Donato's election. Donato's brief reign, lasting little more than a month, is summarized with remarks on his character, popularity, and sudden death from apoplexy. Wotton concludes by recounting the subsequent election of Antonio Priuli, whose unanimous selection contrasts with the failure of his rivals, and notes the simultaneous death of an Austrian commissioner engaged in negotiations over the Uskok conflict.
mentions: Senate of the Republic of Venice

letters.abstract: Henry Wotton reports recent political developments in Venice, noting the deaths of two dukes and the election of two others within a six-week period. He then describes the city's alarm following the discovery of a major French conspiracy against the Venetian Republic. According to Wotton, numerous conspirators have already been executed by a variety of means, while the full extent of the plot remains unknown.He closes by promising a fuller account of the affair in a subsequent letter and with a prayer for his correspondent's well-being.

letters.abstract: Wotton writes thanking his unnamed correspondent for a certain great honor that, in the end, Wotton was unable to receive. Smith identifies the correspondent as Robert Naunton. The honor, according to Smith, was that Naunton had attempted to get Wotton appointed as Thomas Lake's successor for Secretary of State. letters.abstract: Writing from Padua on 11/21 March 1619, Henry Wotton acknowledges Robert Naunton's letter of 16 February informing him that James I has withdrawn his initial instructions regarding Wotton's prospective employment in the Bohemian affair. Wotton notes that the news arrived just in time to prevent him from dispatching a messenger to Prague in accordance with his earlier provisional orders. He explains that he had already delayed action because of persistent reports that the Emperor was either dead or near death. Wotton also mentions recent respiratory difficulties that prompted his temporary stay in Padua and observes that he has already incurred unusual travel expenses in preparation for the mission, expressing confidence that the king will compensate him. He concludes by approving the appointment of the Earl of Doncaster to the Bohemian mission, praising his greater suitability for so important a diplomatic charge while modestly characterizing himself as better fitted for less complex business.

letters.abstract: Henry Wotton acknowledges Robert Naunton's notification of the death of Queen Anne of Denmark and reports his preparations to communicate the news officially to the Venetian government. Having recently returned from Padua, where he underwent medical treatment for a sciatic ailment, Wotton explains that he has placed himself, his household, and his residence in mourning in anticipation of a formal visit of condolence from the Venetian Senate, following diplomatic custom. He defers a fuller account to a forthcoming letter to be carried by a gentleman rather than the ordinary courier. In a postscript, Wotton refutes recent rumours of the Pope's death, stating that his private intelligence confirms the report to be false, while noting that the origins of the rumour are politically significant and will be explained separately for King James I.

letters.abstract: Writing from Augsburg, Henry Wotton informs Robert Naunton of his progress on his diplomatic mission to the Protestant Union. Having learned that the princes of the Union and representatives of the imperial cities are to assemble at Heilbronn around 10 June, Wotton decides to attend the meeting, judging it an opportunity to address the confederated body collectively rather than negotiate separately with its members. He reports that he has dispatched his secretary ahead to the Elector Palatine to make arrangements for the meeting and expects to reach Heilbronn shortly. Wotton notes that he will write a fuller account to King James I by the next post. In a postscript, he remarks on the recent passage of the Venetian ambassador Antonio Donato in Augsburg. Wotton expresses concerns about the ambassador's return to Venice due to troubles regarding Savoy.

letters.abstract: Wotton reports the expected arrival of the pope's new nuncio in Venice, whose principal mission is widely believed to be securing the readmission of the Jesuits to the Venetian Republic. He notes rumours that the nuncio will pursue this objective with both papal authority and personal zeal. Wotton is unsure whether France will support the effort. Wotton situates the campaign within the broader context of the impending canonization of Ignatius of Loyola, observing that the continued exclusion of the Jesuits from Venetian territory would detract from the order's growing prestige, particularly after its restoration in France and Bohemia. Recalling his presence during the Jesuits' expulsion from Venice, Wotton emphatically argues that reversing that decision would undermine the stability of all civil governments. He closes by referring to other dispatches sent to the king.

letters.abstract: Wotton writes to Walter Aston, English ambassador in Spain, proposing a regular exchange of diplomatic intelligence. Having recently returned from Vienna, he recalls sending Aston a cipher and offers to supply news from Venice. He reports tensions between Venice and the Duchy of Milan after the Duke of Feria attempted to move Spanish troops across Venetian territory. The Venetian Senate has refused them permission and assembled a multinational force, including English, French, and Flemish troops, near Martinengo. Although rumours in Venice suggest fighting has occurred, Wotton discounts these reports on the authority of Sir Henry Peyton. Wotton also expresses scepticism that negotiations over the Valtellina will be implemented before the pope's death, believing the parties are deliberately delaying matters in anticipation of a more favourable successor.

letters.abstract: Henry Wotton warns of the political and religious dangers posed by English students studying medicine at Padua. He reports that candidates receiving medical degrees in the College are required to swear an oath of obedience to the Pope, enclosing a printed copy of the oath for the King's examination. Wotton contends that many English students are already Catholics or are converted abroad, commonly proceed to Rome after graduating, and may even receive priestly orders. He argues that Catholic physicians present a particular threat because their profession grants them intimate access to households and dying patients, enabling covert missionary activity and the possible reconciliation of Protestants on their deathbeds. He urges the King to address what he portrays as a widespread and concealed means of advancing Catholic influence in England. The letter concludes with Wotton's recommendation of the bearer, Thomas Lindsay, son of Barnie Lindsay of the King's Chamber, to Calvert's favour.

letters.abstract: Wotton recounts rumours that a consortium of pirates, initially thought to be led by the English renegade Samson, had offered the Venetian Republic a substantial financial donation, loans at favourable interest, and a fleet of armed vessels in exchange for protection and a permanent base. Although he questions the credibility of the report, he notes that the Venetian Senate had resolved to entertain negotiations. He also reports that the dispute between Venice and the Governor of Milan over the transit of troops across the mainland is moving towards settlement, while the Valtellina question remains unresolved owing to the frail health and diminished capacity of the Pope. Finally, Wotton conveys news from Vienna of the death of Charles Bonaventure de Longueval, Count of Bucquoy, and the subsequent defeat of the Imperial army during its retreat from the siege of Nové Hrady (Neuhäusel), expressing hope that these reverses will facilitate Lord Digby's diplomatic mission and recalling his own earlier advice to the Emperor not to rely upon fortune.

letters.incipit: . . . To-morrow we expect here the Marquis de Coeuvre
letters.abstract: This letter reports anticipated diplomatic developments in Venice surrounding the expected arrival of the Marquis de Coeuvre from Rome. Wotton notes that the French resident, Monsieur de Villiers, has announced that Coeuvre is travelling as ambassador extraordinary. Although rumours have associated his mission with the Jesuit question, Wotton records widespread speculation that this serves merely as a pretext for more significant instructions: namely, to assess the Venetian Republic's willingness to support a French military intervention across the Alps to resolve the Valtellina dispute following the stabilization of France under Louis XIII.

letters.incipit: Right Honourable, The Marquis de Coevre (as I wrote in my former) arrived here on Thursday
letters.abstract: Wotton reports the arrival and formal reception in Venice of the Marquis de Cœuvres, whose public audience with the French resident was marked by conspicuously rigid ceremonial behaviour. Because the marquis’s credentials were not read and subsequent private audiences were delayed by holy days and the election of the new Venetian Senate, Wotton remains unable to determine the substance of his mission, though he doubts that the brief audiences granted to Cœuvres and the papal nuncio could have resolved the complex Jesuit affair. He therefore concentrates on diplomatic precedence. Wotton describes his exchange of visits with Cœuvres and records that the marquis carefully visited him before returning the nuncio’s call, thereby acknowledging the English ambassador’s precedence over the papal representative. He contrasts this settlement with an earlier dispute involving Sir Dudley Carleton and the former French resident, Monsieur de Léon. Wotton concludes with a favourable personal assessment of Cœuvres as respectful toward James I and supportive of Anglo-French amity, though perhaps more forceful in resolution than skilful in negotiation, and notes that he expects soon to use the cipher sent with his previous letter.

letters.abstract: Sarpi ask de Thou if he can help to deliver a copy of the Quran to Isaac Casaubon, who was living in Paris at that time. Sarpi relates that the Quran had been taken as loot some fifty years earlier by Lorenzo Amulio when he had defeated the Turkish corsair Sabbarays.

Sarpi expresses his admiration for Thou's Historiæ sui temporis, a copy of which Thou had sent to him. Given the date of the letter, we can infer that Sarpi is referring to the first part of the history, published in 1604. The second part would not be published until 1606.

Sarpi tells de Thou that the second part of his Historia has been delayed getting to Venice. It is currently in quarantine in Vicentino due to plague worries there. Sarpi offers to give de Thou a careful narration of the tensions between the Pope and Venice for de Thou's use in a subsquent volume of his Historia.
